title: Salary dispute holding up Ollie Bearman’s new Haas F1 deal
article_text:
Motorsport.com understands financial terms are behind the delay in confirming Ollie Bearman for 2027, with Ferrari having already exercised its option on the British driver

Ferrari protege Oliver Bearman remains the only driver on the Formula 1 grid without a contract for 2027. It is a situation that would have been hard to imagine just a few weeks ago, given that his retention at Haas had been taken for granted since last summer.

The announcement of Rafael Camara as Bearman's 2027 team-mate, which came ahead of the Brazilian Grand Prix, was expected to be swiftly followed by that of his British team-mate. Instead, the silence has dragged on to the point of becoming a talking point, even prompting rumours of Bearman driving elsewhere next year. The paradox is that Bearman and Haas have strong reasons to reach an agreement.

Bearman has ruled out racing elsewhere in 2027, while Haas has long been expected to retain him, yet the negotiations have dragged on far longer than initially anticipated.

In recent weeks, there has been speculation about the reasons for the deadlock, some linked to the contractual relationship between Bearman and Ferrari and to the future prospects of the 21-year-old Briton.

According to information obtained by Motorsport.com, however, the issue holding up the signing does not concern the driver’s long-term future, but rather the financial terms of the deal with Haas.

Ferrari has already exercised the option allowing it to retain Bearman within its driver programme. Given that Maranello has invested financial resources in the young Briton ever since he joined the Driver Academy in 2021, allowing Bearman to leave on a free transfer would be a big waste of all those efforts.

Rafael Camara will finish the 2026 season for Haas as he prepares for his full 2027 debut alongside Oliver Bearman.

Bearman could be in a position to leave Ferrari at the end of 2027 if he has not received a call-up to join the works team, but this scenario does not represent an obstacle to renewing with Haas, and there is no need to finalise his relationship with Ferrari in the short term – especially given that Lewis Hamilton is in the twilight of his career. The Scuderia has not ruled out any of its longer-term options.

The immediate negotiations therefore centre on two parties: Haas and Bearman’s entourage. The sticking point is the salary offered by the American team, a figure that the driver and his staff do not consider commensurate with their expectations.

This has led to a prolonged deadlock, despite both sides being aware of the need to reach an agreement. On the eve of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, Bearman made no secret of his disappointment at a situation that has now been dragging on for months. “There’s nothing new to say. To be honest, I’m rather disappointed to find myself here, at the twentieth round of the season, without a signed contract for next year. It’s a strange situation, but we’re getting there.”

The Briton admitted that the uncertainty is becoming difficult to cope with, especially after a season in which he believes he has proved his worth as the team's lead driver.

Bearman categorically ruled out the possibility of moving to another team in 2027, though. When asked if there was even the slightest chance of racing elsewhere, with no more seats up for real discussion, his answer was unequivocal: "No, zero chance."

He added: "My goal for 2027 is very clear. I think we have unfinished business here. Then looking further into the future, it's not really in my hands, let's say it like that."

Bearman has been open about his ambition to make it to Maranello, but he is aware that decisions regarding the Scuderia’s future do not depend solely on his performance.

"Of course I'm under contract with Ferrari. Ferrari have given me this incredible opportunity to step into F1 with them for the first time," he acknowledged. "I'm still a Ferrari junior driver and my ultimate dream is to race for Ferrari. First of all, they're the most iconic team and they're the first team that believed in me as a kid.

"It's still my ultimate dream, but there's no doubt that looking into the future, there may be some challenges there. There's no denying that, it's very clear. I don't really have much say in the matter. We just need to see how things develop over time."

The immediate contract situation is more straightforward. Ferrari has already clarified its contractual position and is not the party holding up Bearman’s confirmation. The ongoing negotiations concern only the terms of the agreement between the driver and Haas. According to information gathered by Motorsport.com, the matter is expected to be resolved before the final weekend in Abu Dhabi, in all likelihood through an inevitable compromise on the financial front.

That doesn't make the lack of a deal by the end of November any less frustrating for Bearman. "It's not a good feeling to be sitting here with two races to go without things sorted out," he said. "Even though I know that we're pretty much there, the fact is that we're not. There's no excuse for being here without a contract signed, quite honestly."

Those comments show just how much this whole tug-of-war has weighed on the driver. Barring an unexpected breakdown in negotiations, Bearman is expected to remain with Haas in 2027 as well, forming one of the youngest driver pairings on the grid alongside Camara.

title: Haas confirm Camara will finish 2026 season with the team
article_text:
Brazilian driver Rafa Camara will complete the 2026 season with Haas ahead of his full rookie season in 2027, the team confirmed on Sunday.

Formula 2 championship leader Camara took the place of ousted Esteban Ocon in Brazil and continued in the seat at this week's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

He will race for the team in Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6. The Ferrari junior had already been confirmed to be replacing Ocon in 2027, but the Frenchman's sudden sacking during the Mexico City Grand Prix accelerated his F1 debut.

Haas' decision will likely cost Camara the chance to be F2 champion. F1's main feeder series will finish its own championship four races spread across the schedule in Qatar and Abu Dhabi -- Camara holds a slender seven-point lead over Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov, with Alpine junior Alex Dunne 18 points back.

Team boss Aayo Komatsu said the opportunity for Camara to embed further into the team was too good to turn down. "We're excited to be able to finish the season with Rafa driving and build on his first two race starts with the team in Brazil and America," Komatsu said.

"I'm delighted that Rafa's embraced every track session as a learning opportunity and embedded himself further within the team. We now get to finish the season together which is advantageous to all of us ahead of a relatively short off-season and as our 2027 preparations get underway."

Haas had one other option if they had wanted Camara to finish off his F2 campaign -- reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa filled in for Ocon in Mexico City and scored a top-ten finish on his debut.

Camara will keep driving alongside fellow Ferrari junior Oliver Bearman in the final races. Although it is expected to be completed soon, Bearman has not had a new Haas deal confirmed yet.

Bearman is understood to be in talks with Ferrari about their wider plans for his career, mindful of what happens with him should Lewis Hamilton extend his stay with the team beyond 2027.

title: F1’s $3.2 Billion Las Vegas Legacy Sets The Stage For Luxury Brands To Up Their Game In 2026
Lewis Hamilton says he could win record eighth F1 championship as Ferrari’s number one driver
article_text:
Lewis Hamilton has suggested that a record-breaking eighth world title would have been within reach this season had Ferrari chosen to prioritise him over team-mate Charles Leclerc.

His comments came after he collided with Leclerc for the second time in three races at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, an incident described as "completely unacceptable" by Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur. Stewards later penalised Leclerc for his role in the collision.

Following his first victory for Ferrari at the seventh round of 23 in Barcelona, Hamilton moved 40 points ahead of Leclerc and sat 41 points adrift of Antonelli.

Although the 41-year-old rejected claims he asked Ferrari to make him their lead driver, he suggested that, with the right backing from his team, he could have given Antonelli a proper run for his money.

"I've never asked to be the number one," said Hamilton. "I genuinely haven't. But there was a point in the season where I was 40 points ahead (of Leclerc) and at that point, the fight was with me and Kimi.

"I was the closest one to him. I was second for a long time in the year, and at that point I needed the backing to make sure we beat Kimi.

"There were a few instances in the season – where, with the support – I think we could have beaten Kimi in that battle.

"It's not what I've asked for. But we shouldn't have been able to come together (in Las Vegas). It should just never happen. I've said everything I can on it. And the question now should be for Ferrari."

Hamilton's chances of finishing runner-up in the standings – his highest championship position since missing out on his eighth title to Max Verstappen in 2021 – now look shot following the Dutch driver's brilliant recent form.

Hamilton is 37 points behind Verstappen with only 50 points left across the remaining rounds, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Hamilton is three points clear of both George Russell and Lando Norris, with Leclerc 17 points adrift.

Russell finished only ninth in Sin City after he pranged the barriers with just two laps remaining when a late move on team-mate Antonelli for second backfired.

"I wanted that win," said Russell. "It was a bizarre race, and I went for a high-risk move and paid the price.

"Of course I'm disappointed with the outcome, however, I have no regrets. I fought and knew if I wanted the win, I needed to be in the top two positions into the final laps."

title: Lewis Hamilton: With #1 driver backing at key points, we could have beaten Kimi Antonelli this season
article_text:
For Ferrari fans. The latest Scuderia Ferrari F1 news, driver updates, technical analysis and race reaction from Maranello and beyond.

Seven-time Formula 1 champion Lewis Hamilton believes he could have beaten Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli in their battle earlier in the season had he been given more support from Ferrari.

The Briton was speaking after the Las Vegas Grand Prix, where he had another clash with his team-mate Charles Leclerc, which sent him into a spin. He recovered to finish seventh, while Leclerc was penalised and finished 10th.

Asked about 1996 F1 champion Damon Hill's suggestion that Ferrari should make him its number one driver, Hamilton said he had never asked for that status, but felt he had needed it earlier in the year.

"I've never asked to be number one. I genuinely haven't ever asked," Hamilton said.

He pointed to a stage of the season when he was well clear of Leclerc and the nearest driver to challenge Antonelli for the title.

"I was second for a long time in the year, and at that point I needed backing to make sure we beat Kimi. There were a few circumstances in the season where, with the support, we could have beaten Kimi," he said.

After the 41-year-old claimed his first grand prix win with Ferrari in Barcelona in June, he was second in the drivers' standings, 41 points behind Antonelli and 40 points ahead of Leclerc. He was also second after Monaco, Belgium and Hungary.

Photo by: Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images

Antonelli went on to secure the championship at the Mexican Grand Prix, one week before Mercedes won the constructors' title, and now has 402 points to Hamilton's 267.

"I don't know, but it's not something I want to get into," he said when asked where his relationship with his team-mate goes from here. "These are questions that people are asking. At the end of the day, I performed as hard as I could, and I've been giving everything I could to get those points today.

"We were just constantly hit with challenges, and I just kept my head down."

Earlier in the race, Hamilton had been handed a 10-second penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage over McLaren's Lando Norris.

"10 seconds was insane and very, very harsh," he continued. "I was avoiding colliding with them, and they could have just told me to give the place back. A 10-second [penalty] is nuts. But I came back and I got back into the fight, and I could see Max up ahead and I was like, we're back in the fight.

"I was fighting with McLaren, so I honestly thought that I could maybe fight for a podium, and I'm literally only thinking about fighting McLaren, because that's where we need to be to get the second."

title: 'The most chaotic race ever' – McLaren's Lando Norris reflects on remarkable recovery to P2 in Las Vegas Grand Prix
article_text:
Lando Norris reflected on an exceptionally chaotic Las Vegas Grand Prix after recovering from outside the points to finish second, securing a double podium for McLaren alongside team mate Oscar Piastri.

Lando Norris has described the Las Vegas Grand Prix as potentially the "most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1" after recovering from outside the points to claim second place and help secure a double podium for McLaren.

The Briton started third but endured a difficult opening stint, slipping as far back as P11 as he struggled with straight-line speed and battery deployment in an eventful race that saw 352 overtakes across the field.

Norris began making progress towards the end of his first stint before a mid-race Safety Car, brought out following a collision between Sergio Perez and Rafael Camara, helped him climb to P6. The McLaren driver continued his recovery after the restart, briefly taking the lead before eventually crossing the line just 0.639s behind race winner Max Verstappen, with team mate Oscar Piastri completing the podium.

"I think that must have been the most chaotic race ever in the history of Formula 1," Norris reflected. "I didn't know what was happening half the time. I didn't know if I was going to have the best race and have a chance to win or end up last.

"I had everything in this race. So it was tough. I timed things well in terms of getting back to the front. It was also a race of not making mistakes, like a lot of people made. So, a fun day. Chaotic, but a fun day, and a good result for us as a team."

Speaking in the post-race press conference, Norris explained that managing his battery deployment had been particularly challenging, leaving him vulnerable to overtakes despite having competitive pace throughout the race.

"Every time I got overtaken, I had no battery, someone else had more battery behind, and I just kept dropping back," he explained.

"The whole race was judging battery the whole time. I'm looking at the battery more than I'm looking where I'm going around this track. So it's the most important thing.

"But the second half of the race was very strong in terms of not making mistakes, staying out of the chaos of some of the others around us, and playing things right in the last three or four laps with positioning, slipstreams and battery to give myself the best chance to finish second."

The result marked Norris' seventh podium of the season and his fifth consecutive top-five finish, with the McLaren driver admitting that he had exceeded his expectations heading into the race.

"Today wasn't a race about trying to win. There was no chance we could win the race today," he said. "But P2 was the best, and we achieved it, so I'm happy."

title: What the teams said – Race day in Las Vegas
article_text:
Verstappen drove a masterclass in Las Vegas to record his third win here and fourth of the season. He led off the line, but was soon challenged by those behind having a tow. Despite losing the lead multiple times, every time the Dutchman kept calm and retook the place. Russell, Norris and Antonelli threw everything they could at the Red Bull man, but no one could make it stick.

Verstappen even had enough composure to debate deployment strategies with the team, worried about being passed last on the final lap and not having time to come back at his rival. But Antonelli’s late issue meant the last lap was the only one where Verstappen had some breathing room from the entire race.

As for Hadjar, his pace was very strong. He ran second and even challenged Verstappen at times. He looked on for a podium until he suffered an apparent front wing failure late on, the resultant pit stop dropping him out of the points. The Frenchman was also handed a 10-second post-race penalty for slowing down before the pit stops, as he attempted to create a gap with Red Bull double stacking their drivers.

“It was definitely one of the craziest Grands Prix I’ve ever experienced. The whole race was about managing the deployment, timing everything correctly and making sure you stayed ahead of the cars behind. They were constantly changing their strategy as well, so you always had to be aware of what was happening around you and make the right decisions. I just wanted to stay in the lead and not drop back into the pack. It was very unusual today and something completely different to what we normally experience, but the most important thing is that we won. We’ve been strong over the last few races, consistently scoring podiums, and the turnaround from the team has been very positive. We did everything right today and I’m happy we came away with the win.”

“A disappointing end to what was a really promising first half of the race. The start was great, and it was fun to be part of what was a crazy battle. We were fighting at the front and had a lot of pace. Unfortunately, the front wing took unexpected damage and we had to box, which took us out of the fight for at least a podium. We knew we’d be fast here, and we were. The car felt so strong through the corners and, with the natural tow, we were able to keep up on the straights. It’s a shame, as everything was looking great, but that’s racing sometimes.”

“What an incredible race and an outstanding performance from Max and the entire Team. We knew that energy management and the slipstream would play a significant role today, but I don't think anyone anticipated quite so much overtaking. Max was simply exceptional, both in attack and defence, keeping his composure right until the very last lap. The communication between Max, his engineers and the pit wall was outstanding, and that teamwork made a real difference in such an unpredictable race.

"At the same time, it is a real shame for Isack. He had fantastic pace, was right up there with Max and at one stage we were running P1 and P2. He deserved so much more from this weekend, and we owe him an apology for what happened today. we will analyse what happened with his front wing and come back stronger in Doha.

"We started the weekend on the back foot, but the way everyone responded, took risks and worked together to turn things around was remarkable. This victory is another fantastic reward for the hard work of everyone in the Team.

"We will enjoy the moment tonight, but then our focus will turn to the last two races of the season and trying to perform at that level again there.”

Norris started from P3, but he struggled on the soft tyres and dropped all the way out of the top 10 in the first stint. Piastri was going better on the mediums and soon climbed back into the top 10 and was even running ahead of his team mate at times. Somehow despite multiple moves, those two kept their battles clean.

The Australian lost out in the double stack behind the Safety Car, but soon climbed back to where his team mate was running. On the mediums, they looked much more competitive and weaved their way forward, with Norris even picking off Russell and Verstappen and leading for a few corners at one point.

They were behind the two Mercedes cars when Russell ran off, and both picked off Antonelli right at the end to score what, at times this weekend, looked a very unlikely double podium.

“It was a chaotic race from start to finish, and every lap brought something to manage: battery use, positioning, slipstreams and whether to attack or defend. I was down the order early on, and it took time to understand how to use the battery and get the most from the car. Once we worked that out, we started making progress. The cornering speed was strong, but our lack of straight-line speed made it difficult to move forward and hold position. We timed the opportunities well, especially in the closing laps, and second place was the best we could achieve. I’m very happy for the team to come away with a double podium.
